screens.title: Layer 2 Threat Mitigation Techniques
screens.narratorSegment: Layer 2 weaknesses are often the most practical path for an attacker to enter an enterprise network. In this lesson we will examine three common attack classes—ARP spoofing, DHCP spoofing, and MAC flooding—and the Catalyst switch features that stop them. You will learn how DHCP Snooping builds a trusted binding database, how Dynamic ARP Inspection validates ARP traffic against that database, how IP Source Guard enforces source IP/MAC bindings on access ports, and how Port Security limits MAC learning to prevent table exhaustion. Each feature has a clear role and dependency: DHCP Snooping must be active for DAI and IPSG to work correctly. We will also walk through a concise configuration and verification workflow for a real-world access port scenario so you can apply these controls safely. By the end of the chapter you will understand not only commands, but the rationale behind trusted and untrusted ports, the common pitfalls that break deployments, and the right verification steps to avoid locking out legitimate users. Think about the last time you troubleshooted user connectivity; these tools give you both protection and evidence to diagnose access-layer faults.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.5 › Layer 2 Threat Mitigation Techniques
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Layer 2 Threat Mitigation Techniques

Learn the set of access-layer defenses on Cisco Catalyst switches that block rogue DHCP servers, ARP poisoning, IP/MAC spoofing, and MAC table exhaustion. We'll connect commands to outcomes so you can both configure and verify safely.

In this lesson
Practical CLI workflow, binding database, trust model, and verification
Coming up
DHCP Snooping
Filters DHCP replies and builds a binding database used by other security features.
Dynamic ARP Inspection
Validates ARP packets against the DHCP snooping database to block ARP spoofing.
IP Source Guard & Port Security
Enforce IP/MAC bindings and limit MAC learning to stop spoofing and flooding.
Practical outcome

You will be able to configure and verify protections on an access port and reason about trusted vs untrusted uplinks.

Concept Map
DHCP Snooping
Trusted/untrusted ports and binding database
DAI
ARP validation using DHCP database
IPSG & Port Security
Source verification and MAC limits
Quick tip
Always mark uplinks to DHCP servers and other infrastructure as trusted. Missing a trusted port is the most common cause of failed deployments.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this first objectives slide we'll establish the core practical skills you'll need. First, you will be able to explain Layer 2 vulnerabilities such as ARP spoofing, DHCP spoofing, and MAC flooding with clear examples of the attacker goals and impact. Understanding these attacks matters because they compromise traffic integrity and network availability at the access layer. Second, you will learn to enable and configure DHCP Snooping so the switch filters rogue DHCP replies and builds the binding database. This is a hands-on skill: a correct configuration distinguishes trusted uplinks from untrusted access ports and prevents rogue servers from assigning malicious network settings. Third, you will implement Dynamic ARP Inspection, which uses the DHCP Snooping bindings to validate ARP messages and stop ARP poisoning. Finally, you will deploy IP Source Guard to prevent IP and MAC spoofing per access port. For each objective we include a small mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember why the feature matters and a verified competency milestone to show practical mastery.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on port controls, the order of operations, and operational verification. You will configure Port Security to limit the number of MAC addresses on access ports and use sticky or static MAC entries to control which devices are permitted. Understanding violation modes is crucial: shutdown is the most secure but can easily disable legitimate access if used without monitoring; restrict and protect offer graduated responses. Next, you will learn the interaction and order of operations: DHCP Snooping must be configured and populated so DAI and IPSG can validate mappings. We will practice adding static bindings when devices use fixed IP addresses, because DAI will otherwise drop ARP for those hosts. Finally, you will gain the ability to verify behavior using show commands such as show ip dhcp snooping binding, show ip arp inspection, show ip verify source, and show port-security. These verification steps are not optional; they prove the binding database exists and that enforcement is active. Each card includes a short mnemonic and a competency milestone so you can track mastery.

screens.title: DHCP Snooping: purpose and configuration
screens.narratorSegment: DHCP Snooping acts as the first line of defense at the access layer by filtering DHCP server messages and creating a trusted binding database. At its core it classifies ports as trusted or untrusted. Trusted ports connect to legitimate DHCP servers or upstream infrastructure; untrusted ports connect to end-user devices. When enabled, the switch drops DHCP server replies that arrive on untrusted ports, preventing a rogue machine from offering incorrect IP addresses, gateways, or DNS settings. Practically, you enable DHCP Snooping globally, enable it per VLAN, and mark uplinks to your DHCP server as trusted. You can also rate-limit DHCP messages on untrusted ports to defend against DHCP starvation attacks. A very common operational mistake is forgetting to mark the uplink as trusted, which causes legitimate DHCP replies to be dropped. To make this concrete, imagine a PC obtaining an IP in VLAN 10 via a legitimate server on the core switch. If Gi1/0/24—your uplink—is not trusted, DHCP replies will be dropped and the client will fail to obtain an address. Before enabling enforcement-dependent features like DAI and IPSG, confirm the binding database with show ip dhcp snooping binding. That verification both demonstrates success and provides the exact MAC–IP–VLAN mapping DAI and IPSG rely on. Do you have a plan to mark only true server-facing ports as trusted in your access design?

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.5 › DHCP Snooping
Configuration snippet
enable configure terminal vlan 10 name DEPARTMENT_VLAN exit ip dhcp snooping ip dhcp snooping vlan 10 interface GigabitEthernet1/0/24 description Uplink to Core (DHCP Server) switchport mode trunk ip dhcp snooping trust no shutdown interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1 description End-user Workstation Port switchport mode access switchport access vlan 10 no shutdown ! Optional: rate limit DHCP on untrusted port interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1 ip dhcp snooping limit rate 15
Keep the binding database visible with show ip dhcp snooping binding to confirm clients obtained addresses via the trusted server.
How it helps
  • Blocks DHCP server replies on untrusted ports so rogue servers cannot provide malicious configuration.
  • Builds a binding table mapping MAC, IP, VLAN, interface, and lease time for each DHCP client.
  • Provides the authoritative data other features use to validate ARP and source addresses.
Common mistake
Forgetting to mark the DHCP server uplink as trusted will block legitimate DHCP replies. Verify trusted ports after configuration.
Key Takeaway

DHCP Snooping must be enabled and properly trusted before enabling DAI or IPSG, because they rely on its binding database.

screens.title: Binding database, trust model, and rate limits
screens.narratorSegment: The binding database is the practical output of DHCP Snooping and is the foundation for DAI and IP Source Guard. Each binding record contains a client MAC address, leased IP, VLAN, interface, lease time, and binding type. The switch learns these when a client successfully completes DHCP. Think of the binding table as a ledger: it records who received which IP and where. A deployment checklist should include marking upstream device ports as trusted, enabling snooping for the VLANs you manage, and confirming the binding table populates during client DHCP transactions. Rate limiting is an important defensive layer: an attacker can attempt DHCP starvation by sending many DHCP discovery messages to exhaust available leases or flood the DHCP server with bogus requests. You can configure ip dhcp snooping limit rate on untrusted ports to cap the number of DHCP messages per second. A concrete example: if an access port serves a workstation use a conservative limit like 10–15 messages per second to prevent accidental or malicious storms while still allowing legitimate client renewals. Misconception to avoid: rate limits do not replace marking trusted ports. If you apply rate limits incorrectly on an uplink, you can impact legitimate DHCP traffic. End with the habit: always verify bindings with show ip dhcp snooping binding and inspect bindings before enabling features that will enforce them.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.5 › Binding Database & Rate Limits
Binding record fields
  • Client MAC address
  • IP address and lease time
  • VLAN and interface where the lease was observed
  • Binding type (DHCP learned or static)
Use the binding data to validate ARP and to create static entries for devices that use fixed IPs.
Rate limiting DHCP messages
Apply ip dhcp snooping limit rate on untrusted access ports to defend against DHCP starvation attempts. Typical values for single-host access ports are 10–20 messages per second; tune based on renewal behavior in your network.
Operational note
Rate limiting must be applied only to untrusted ports. Do not enable on uplinks to servers, or you could throttle legitimate DHCP traffic.
Check your understanding
After enabling DHCP Snooping, run show ip dhcp snooping binding and confirm the client MAC and IP appear for the expected interface. If static IP hosts exist, add static bindings manually so enforcement features will allow their traffic.
Key Takeaway

The binding database is the single source of truth for later ARP and source checks; populate and verify it before turning on enforcement.

screens.title: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI)
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic ARP Inspection prevents ARP poisoning by validating ARP requests and replies against known bindings. ARP spoofing works because hosts accept gratuitous ARP replies; an attacker can claim someone else's IP and receive traffic meant for that IP. DAI inspects ARP packets on untrusted ports and compares the source IP-to-MAC mapping to the DHCP snooping binding database. If the mapping does not match, or the ARP packet presents an unexpected static mapping, the switch drops the packet. You enable DAI per VLAN and mark infrastructure ports as trusted so legitimate ARP traffic from upstream devices is not inspected. DAI offers validation options such as src-mac, dst-mac, and ip checks depending on how strict you want checks to be. A concrete example: a client with MAC 00AA.00BB.00CC that obtained IP 10.0.10.5 will have an entry in the binding database; any ARP mapping that claims 10.0.10.5 from a different MAC will be dropped. A common misconception is that DAI protects devices with static IPs automatically; it does not. Static hosts require manual DHCP snooping static bindings or static ARP entries so DAI can validate them. Always confirm that the binding database contains entries for static hosts before enforcing DAI to avoid dropping legitimate ARP traffic.

keyIdea.title: DAI depends on DHCP Snooping
keyIdea.text: DAI validates ARP packets against the DHCP snooping binding table; static IP hosts must have manual bindings for DAI to allow their ARP traffic.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.5 › Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI)
What DAI checks
  • Validates ARP requests and replies against DHCP Snooping bindings
  • Can validate source MAC, destination MAC, and IP fields
  • Drops ARP packets with mappings that do not match bindings
Enable with ip arp inspection vlan & mark trusted ports with ip arp inspection trust for uplinks and inter-switch links.
Example
Client MAC 00AA.00BB.00CC gets 10.0.10.5 via DHCP. DAI will drop ARP packets that claim 10.0.10.5 from any other MAC address.
Common misconception
DAI does not automatically know about static IP assignments; you must create static DHCP bindings or configure static ARP entries so DAI can validate those hosts.
Key Takeaway

Enable DHCP Snooping first. DAI uses that table to stop forged ARP and requires manual bindings for static hosts.

screens.title: IP Source Guard (IPSG)
screens.narratorSegment: IP Source Guard enforces that traffic leaving an access port can only use the source IP and MAC recorded in the DHCP Snooping binding database or a configured static binding. Essentially, when you enable IPSG on a port, the switch creates an implicit port access control list that filters traffic by source. You can run IPSG in IP-only mode, which checks the source IP, or in IP-MAC mode, which checks both IP and MAC. IP-MAC mode provides stronger protection because it prevents a host from changing either identifier to impersonate another device. For devices with static IP addresses, IPSG requires a static binding in the DHCP Snooping database; otherwise IPSG will drop their traffic. A practical example: enable ip verify source port-security on an access interface where port security is already used. If a workstation uses DHCP, IPSG accepts the client's traffic because the binding exists. If an attacker plugs in and spoofs that IP, IPSG drops the traffic. A common pitfall is enabling IPSG without verifying binding entries—this often results in legitimate hosts being blocked. The operational advice is to confirm bindings and, if needed, add static entries for servers and network devices before enabling IPSG enforcement.

keyIdea.title: IPSG in practice
keyIdea.text: IPSG filters traffic on a per-port basis using the DHCP Snooping database; configure mode and static bindings carefully to avoid blocking legitimate hosts.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.5 › IP Source Guard
Modes and behavior
  • IP-only: verifies only the source IP matches the binding
  • IP-MAC: verifies both IP and MAC; stronger protection
  • Works per access port and creates an implicit port ACL based on bindings
Command example: ip verify source port-security on the interface. Ensure DHCP Snooping bindings exist for DHCP clients; add static bindings for fixed-IP devices.
Example scenario
A workstation that obtained 10.0.10.5 via DHCP is allowed. If an attacker plugs in and spoofs 10.0.10.5 from a different MAC, IPSG drops the spoofed traffic because it doesn't match the binding for that interface.
Remember: add static bindings for servers or devices using static IPs so they pass IPSG checks.
Key Takeaway

IPSG is a per-port defense that stops hosts from claiming IP/MAC identities they do not own. Validate bindings and add static entries before enforcement.

screens.title: Port Security and MAC flooding mitigation
screens.narratorSegment: Port Security protects against MAC flooding by limiting the number of MAC addresses that can be learned on a port and by allowing you to bind specific MAC addresses to a port. The goal is to prevent an attacker from sending many forged source MAC addresses to exhaust the switch MAC table, forcing the switch into a hub-like flooding behavior. To configure, set the port to access mode, enable switchport port-security, choose the maximum number of MAC addresses, and decide whether to use sticky learning or static MAC assignments. Sticky MAC learns addresses and writes them into the running config so they persist until explicitly cleared. Violation modes determine the operational response: shutdown disables the port and is most secure, restrict drops violating frames and increments counters, and protect simply drops violating frames silently. A frequent mistake is enabling shutdown without monitoring; a legitimate user attaching multiple devices could unintentionally disable the port and impact operations. In an access-port example allow two sticky MACs and set violation restrict to log events without shutting down. Use show port-security to inspect learned MACs and violation counters. Port Security complements DHCP Snooping, DAI, and IPSG by limiting the number of possible attacker identities on a single port.

keyIdea.title: Port Security best practices
keyIdea.text: Use sticky MACs for endpoint stability, choose restrict for production to avoid accidental shutdowns, and monitor port-security counters regularly.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.5 › Port Security
Configuration pattern
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1 switchport mode access switchport access vlan 10 switchport port-security switchport port-security maximum 2 switchport port-security mac-address sticky switchport port-security violation restrict
Sticky mode simplifies device onboarding. Consider restrict for production to avoid accidental outages from shutdown mode.
Violation mode comparison
  • Shutdown: disables the port on violation (most secure)
  • Restrict: drops violating traffic and increments counters (recommended for production)
  • Protect: drops violating traffic silently without counters
Why it matters
By limiting MAC learning on an access port you reduce the attack surface for MAC flooding. Combined with DHCP Snooping and IPSG, Port Security ensures only expected endpoints can transmit and limits attacker identity spoofing.

screens.title: Feature interaction and order of operations
screens.narratorSegment: These Layer 2 security features form a layered defense, but order matters. DHCP Snooping must be enabled and must populate the binding database before Dynamic ARP Inspection or IP Source Guard can validate traffic. Think about the binding database as the single source of truth: DAI consults it to validate ARP entries and IPSG uses it to construct port-level source filters. Port Security operates somewhat independently, limiting MAC learning at a port, but it is complementary: by limiting the number of MACs, port security reduces the potential for an attacker to inject many identities that would otherwise attempt DHCP or ARP spoofing. A practical deployment sequence is: enable DHCP Snooping globally and per relevant VLAN; verify bindings populate from legitimate DHCP transactions; enable DAI per VLAN and trust uplinks; enable IPSG on access ports (in IP-MAC mode when appropriate); and finally enable Port Security with a sensible violation mode. A common operational trap is to enable DAI or IPSG before checking for static hosts; those hosts must have static bindings or their ARP and traffic will be dropped. For maintainability, document trusted ports and any static bindings so future changes do not inadvertently break access. What documentation will you keep alongside these configurations to prevent accidental outages?

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.5 › Feature Interaction
Recommended deployment order
  1. Enable ip dhcp snooping globally and per VLAN and mark trusted ports.
  2. Confirm binding entries populate with show ip dhcp snooping binding.
  3. Enable ip arp inspection vlan and mark trusted uplinks for DAI.
  4. Enable ip verify source on access ports (IP-MAC mode when possible).
  5. Configure switchport port-security with appropriate maximum and violation mode.
Document trusted ports and static bindings to prevent accidental traffic drops when enforcement is enabled.
Complementary protections
DHCP Snooping builds the database. DAI validates ARP. IPSG filters source IP/MAC. Port Security limits MAC learning. Together they reduce spoofing, poisoning, and flooding risks.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.5 › Hands-on Lab
Lab configuration (SW1)
! SW1 Configuration
enable
configure terminal

! Define VLAN 10
vlan 10
 name DEPARTMENT_VLAN
exit

! Step 1: Enable DHCP Snooping globally and for VLAN 10
ip dhcp snooping
ip dhcp snooping vlan 10

! Step 2 & 3: Configure Gi1/0/24 as trusted for DHCP Snooping and DAI
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/24
 description Uplink to Core (DHCP Server)
 switchport mode trunk ! Assuming it's a trunk to carry multiple VLANs
 ip dhcp snooping trust
 ip arp inspection trust
 no shutdown

! Step 4: Configure Gi1/0/1 as access port in VLAN 10
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
 description End-user Workstation Port
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 no shutdown

! Step 5: Enable IP Source Guard (IP-MAC mode) on Gi1/0/1
 ip verify source port-security

! Step 6: Enable Port Security on Gi1/0/1
 switchport port-security
 switchport port-security maximum 2
 switchport port-security mac-address sticky
 switchport port-security violation restrict

end
write memory
Verification commands
After connecting a client and obtaining DHCP, run these commands to confirm behavior:
  • show ip dhcp snooping binding
  • show ip arp inspection vlan 10
  • show ip verify source interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
  • show port-security interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
Try connecting a third device to Gi1/0/1; with maximum 2 and violation restrict, traffic from the third device will be dropped and counters incremented.
Key Takeaway

Run verification commands after configuration. If static hosts exist, add static bindings before enabling enforcement to prevent unintended service disruption.

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to fix them
screens.narratorSegment: When deploying Layer 2 security, common mistakes are predictable and avoidable if you follow verification steps. The first mistake is failing to mark uplinks as trusted. This causes legitimate DHCP replies to be dropped and prevents binding table population, cascading into DAI and IPSG failures. Remedy: verify ip dhcp snooping trust on the uplink and check binding entries for client MACs. The second mistake is enabling DAI or IPSG while static IP hosts lack static bindings. DAI will drop ARP for those hosts and IPSG will block their traffic. Remedy: add static entries to the DHCP snooping binding database using the ip dhcp snooping binding command or use static ARP entries where appropriate. The third operational trap is using shutdown violation mode on port security in a busy environment without monitoring. A user plugging multiple devices or a legitimate phone and PC can disable the port unexpectedly. Remedy: use restrict and monitor port-security counters, then consider shutdown only with automated remediation or strict access control. Finally, misapplied rate-limits on uplinks can throttle legitimate DHCP traffic; apply rate limiting only on untrusted access ports. After any change, run the key show commands to confirm the expected state and keep configuration notes documenting trusted ports and static bindings to avoid surprises during maintenance.

Module 08 › Chapter 8.5 › Common Mistakes
Mistake
Uplink not trusted
Symptom: no bindings, DHCP failures. Fix: mark uplink with ip dhcp snooping trust and ip arp inspection trust, then re-test DHCP.
Mistake
Static IPs without bindings
Symptom: static hosts blocked by DAI/IPSG. Fix: add ip dhcp snooping binding entries for static hosts or create trusted static ARP entries.
Mistake
Aggressive violation mode
Symptom: ports shut and outages. Fix: use restrict for production, monitor counters, and reserve shutdown for controlled environments.
Action checklist
  • Confirm trusted ports and binding entries before enabling DAI/IPSG.
  • Add static bindings for devices with fixed IPs.
  • Choose port-security violation modes that match your operational tolerance and monitor logs.
  • Apply DHCP rate limits only on untrusted access ports.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These three compact ideas capture the practical essence of Layer 2 threat mitigation. First, DHCP Snooping is the foundational feature that filters DHCP server replies and builds the binding database; it must be enabled and populated before other enforcement features. Second, Dynamic ARP Inspection uses that binding database to validate ARP and prevent ARP spoofing, but static hosts require manual bindings. Third, IP Source Guard and Port Security enforce source identity and limit MAC learning at the port, blocking spoofing and MAC flooding. Together these features form an integrated defense: DHCP Snooping supplies trusted mappings, DAI and IPSG enforce them, and Port Security limits the number of possible attacker identities on a port. Always verify with show commands and document trusted ports and static bindings to avoid operational surprises. fullNarratorScript:
Layer 2 weaknesses are often the most practical path for an attacker to enter an enterprise network. In this lesson we will examine three common attack classes—ARP spoofing, DHCP spoofing, and MAC flooding—and the Catalyst switch features that stop them. You will learn how DHCP Snooping builds a trusted binding database, how Dynamic ARP Inspection validates ARP traffic against that database, how IP Source Guard enforces source IP/MAC bindings on access ports, and how Port Security limits MAC learning to prevent table exhaustion. Each feature has a clear role and dependency: DHCP Snooping must be active for DAI and IPSG to work correctly. We will also walk through a concise configuration and verification workflow for a real-world access port scenario so you can apply these controls safely. By the end of the chapter you will understand not only commands, but the rationale behind trusted and untrusted ports, the common pitfalls that break deployments, and the right verification steps to avoid locking out legitimate users. Think about the last time you troubleshooted user connectivity; these tools give you both protection and evidence to diagnose access-layer faults.

In this first objectives slide we'll establish the core practical skills you'll need. First, you will be able to explain Layer 2 vulnerabilities such as ARP spoofing, DHCP spoofing, and MAC flooding with clear examples of the attacker goals and impact. Understanding these attacks matters because they compromise traffic integrity and network availability at the access layer. Second, you will learn to enable and configure DHCP Snooping so the switch filters rogue DHCP replies and builds the binding database. This is a hands-on skill: a correct configuration distinguishes trusted uplinks from untrusted access ports and prevents rogue servers from assigning malicious network settings. Third, you will implement Dynamic ARP Inspection, which uses the DHCP Snooping bindings to validate ARP messages and stop ARP poisoning. Finally, you will deploy IP Source Guard to prevent IP and MAC spoofing per access port. For each objective we include a small mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember why the feature matters and a verified competency milestone to show practical mastery.

This second objectives slide focuses on port controls, the order of operations, and operational verification. You will configure Port Security to limit the number of MAC addresses on access ports and use sticky or static MAC entries to control which devices are permitted. Understanding violation modes is crucial: shutdown is the most secure but can easily disable legitimate access if used without monitoring; restrict and protect offer graduated responses. Next, you will learn the interaction and order of operations: DHCP Snooping must be configured and populated so DAI and IPSG can validate mappings. We will practice adding static bindings when devices use fixed IP addresses, because DAI will otherwise drop ARP for those hosts. Finally, you will gain the ability to verify behavior using show commands such as show ip dhcp snooping binding, show ip arp inspection, show ip verify source, and show port-security. These verification steps are not optional; they prove the binding database exists and that enforcement is active. Each card includes a short mnemonic and a competency milestone so you can track mastery.

DHCP Snooping acts as the first line of defense at the access layer by filtering DHCP server messages and creating a trusted binding database. At its core it classifies ports as trusted or untrusted. Trusted ports connect to legitimate DHCP servers or upstream infrastructure; untrusted ports connect to end-user devices. When enabled, the switch drops DHCP server replies that arrive on untrusted ports, preventing a rogue machine from offering incorrect IP addresses, gateways, or DNS settings. Practically, you enable DHCP Snooping globally, enable it per VLAN, and mark uplinks to your DHCP server as trusted. You can also rate-limit DHCP messages on untrusted ports to defend against DHCP starvation attacks. A very common operational mistake is forgetting to mark the uplink as trusted, which causes legitimate DHCP replies to be dropped. To make this concrete, imagine a PC obtaining an IP in VLAN 10 via a legitimate server on the core switch. If Gi1/0/24—your uplink—is not trusted, DHCP replies will be dropped and the client will fail to obtain an address. Before enabling enforcement-dependent features like DAI and IPSG, confirm the binding database with show ip dhcp snooping binding. That verification both demonstrates success and provides the exact MAC–IP–VLAN mapping DAI and IPSG rely on. Do you have a plan to mark only true server-facing ports as trusted in your access design?

The binding database is the practical output of DHCP Snooping and is the foundation for DAI and IP Source Guard. Each binding record contains a client MAC address, leased IP, VLAN, interface, lease time, and binding type. The switch learns these when a client successfully completes DHCP. Think of the binding table as a ledger: it records who received which IP and where. A deployment checklist should include marking upstream device ports as trusted, enabling snooping for the VLANs you manage, and confirming the binding table populates during client DHCP transactions. Rate limiting is an important defensive layer: an attacker can attempt DHCP starvation by sending many DHCP discovery messages to exhaust available leases or flood the DHCP server with bogus requests. You can configure ip dhcp snooping limit rate on untrusted ports to cap the number of DHCP messages per second. A concrete example: if an access port serves a workstation use a conservative limit like 10–15 messages per second to prevent accidental or malicious storms while still allowing legitimate client renewals. Misconception to avoid: rate limits do not replace marking trusted ports. If you apply rate limits incorrectly on an uplink, you can impact legitimate DHCP traffic. End with the habit: always verify bindings with show ip dhcp snooping binding and inspect bindings before enabling features that will enforce them.

Dynamic ARP Inspection prevents ARP poisoning by validating ARP requests and replies against known bindings. ARP spoofing works because hosts accept gratuitous ARP replies; an attacker can claim someone else's IP and receive traffic meant for that IP. DAI inspects ARP packets on untrusted ports and compares the source IP-to-MAC mapping to the DHCP snooping binding database. If the mapping does not match, or the ARP packet presents an unexpected static mapping, the switch drops the packet. You enable DAI per VLAN and mark infrastructure ports as trusted so legitimate ARP traffic from upstream devices is not inspected. DAI offers validation options such as src-mac, dst-mac, and ip checks depending on how strict you want checks to be. A concrete example: a client with MAC 00AA.00BB.00CC that obtained IP 10.0.10.5 will have an entry in the binding database; any ARP mapping that claims 10.0.10.5 from a different MAC will be dropped. A common misconception is that DAI protects devices with static IPs automatically; it does not. Static hosts require manual DHCP snooping static bindings or static ARP entries so DAI can validate them. Always confirm that the binding database contains entries for static hosts before enforcing DAI to avoid dropping legitimate ARP traffic.

IP Source Guard enforces that traffic leaving an access port can only use the source IP and MAC recorded in the DHCP Snooping binding database or a configured static binding. Essentially, when you enable IPSG on a port, the switch creates an implicit port access control list that filters traffic by source. You can run IPSG in IP-only mode, which checks the source IP, or in IP-MAC mode, which checks both IP and MAC. IP-MAC mode provides stronger protection because it prevents a host from changing either identifier to impersonate another device. For devices with static IP addresses, IPSG requires a static binding in the DHCP Snooping database; otherwise IPSG will drop their traffic. A practical example: enable ip verify source port-security on an access interface where port security is already used. If a workstation uses DHCP, IPSG accepts the client's traffic because the binding exists. If an attacker plugs in and spoofs that IP, IPSG drops the traffic. A common pitfall is enabling IPSG without verifying binding entries—this often results in legitimate hosts being blocked. The operational advice is to confirm bindings and, if needed, add static entries for servers and network devices before enabling IPSG enforcement.

Port Security protects against MAC flooding by limiting the number of MAC addresses that can be learned on a port and by allowing you to bind specific MAC addresses to a port. The goal is to prevent an attacker from sending many forged source MAC addresses to exhaust the switch MAC table, forcing the switch into a hub-like flooding behavior. To configure, set the port to access mode, enable switchport port-security, choose the maximum number of MAC addresses, and decide whether to use sticky learning or static MAC assignments. Sticky MAC learns addresses and writes them into the running config so they persist until explicitly cleared. Violation modes determine the operational response: shutdown disables the port and is most secure, restrict drops violating frames and increments counters, and protect simply drops violating frames silently. A frequent mistake is enabling shutdown without monitoring; a legitimate user attaching multiple devices could unintentionally disable the port and impact operations. In an access-port example allow two sticky MACs and set violation restrict to log events without shutting down. Use show port-security to inspect learned MACs and violation counters. Port Security complements DHCP Snooping, DAI, and IPSG by limiting the number of possible attacker identities on a single port.

These Layer 2 security features form a layered defense, but order matters. DHCP Snooping must be enabled and must populate the binding database before Dynamic ARP Inspection or IP Source Guard can validate traffic. Think about the binding database as the single source of truth: DAI consults it to validate ARP entries and IPSG uses it to construct port-level source filters. Port Security operates somewhat independently, limiting MAC learning at a port, but it is complementary: by limiting the number of MACs, port security reduces the potential for an attacker to inject many identities that would otherwise attempt DHCP or ARP spoofing. A practical deployment sequence is: enable DHCP Snooping globally and per relevant VLAN; verify bindings populate from legitimate DHCP transactions; enable DAI per VLAN and trust uplinks; enable IPSG on access ports (in IP-MAC mode when appropriate); and finally enable Port Security with a sensible violation mode. A common operational trap is to enable DAI or IPSG before checking for static hosts; those hosts must have static bindings or their ARP and traffic will be dropped. For maintainability, document trusted ports and any static bindings so future changes do not inadvertently break access. What documentation will you keep alongside these configurations to prevent accidental outages?
